newsitem.title: USA: SBC has tough explaining to win AT&T merger.
newsitem.headline: SBC has tough explaining to win AT&T merger.

text.p: Telephone giants SBC and AT&T Corp. will have to do some tough explaining to persuade regulators to allow their proposed merger to go ahead, legal experts say.
The same compelling documents that persuaded regulators to let SBC merge with Pacific Telesis earlier this year are damning when it comes to a potential combination with AT&T, they say.

Basking Ridge, N.J.-based AT&T is in talks to merge with San Antonio, Texas-based SBC -- currently the largest provider of local phone service -- in what would be an estimated $50 billion-plus transaction. It would be the biggest such deal in history.

But the deal faces tough scrutiny from government regulators intent on preventing creation of a new telecommunications "monolith" such as AT&T was before the historic 1982 court ruling that created the "Baby Bell" local phone companies and limited "Ma Bell" to the long-distance phone market.

However, since passage of the most recent federal telecommunications law, there has been an explosion in merger activity throughout the industry, with "Baby Bells" combining to form regional or even multi-regional telecom giants.

When SBC was preparing its recent merger with Pacific Telesis, it made the case that its partner was not a potential competitor -- which would have made it ineligible for merger -- because the real competitors waiting in the wings were the big long-distance companies, led by AT&T.

In documents filed with the California Public Utilities Commission on Dec. 20, SBC and Pacific Telesis noted that AT&T and other long-distance firms had announced plans to become aggressive players in the local exchange market. "Many documents demonstrate AT&T's and MCI's commitment to entering the local exchange" market, the brief said.
"These documents hurt," antitrust and communications lawyer Steve Sunshine said of the effect of the documents on the proposal to merge SBC and AT&T.
Until now, local phone companies have not really had competitors. But last year's telecommunications law was designed to encourage competition in local phone service.
The law is designed to dovetail with the nation's antitrust laws, which prohibit the merger of potential competitors when there are only a few firms in a market.

"In the real world there's nobody else out there for competition that has the AT&T brand name and physical presence in the market," Sunshine said. AT&T has large, expensive switching facilities all over the country, financial resources and "internal scope and scale."

Again, it is SBC itself that makes the point. An SBC expert, Richard Gilbert, said on July 3, 1996, in testimony before the California Public Utilities Comission: "Perhaps no firm has more telecommunications facilities, customers, or name recognition than AT&T."

Despite that, almost as soon as the ink was dry on the SBC-Pacific Telesis merger -- giving it the franchises for local service in California, Texas and five other states -- SBC huddled to talk merger with AT&T, the nation's biggest carrier of long-distance calls.
So, what can SBC say now?
"The argument has got to be there are lots of other people who can get in there and keep the market competitive," Sunshine said.
That is what SBC intends to do. "They are going to offer a comprehensive plan that would make this deal pro-competitive," a source close to the negotiations said.
SBC can then argue, as it did previously, that there are many potential competitors for local service.
However, none of those SBC mentioned in earlier filings -- such as Metropolitan Fiber Systems, Brooks Fiber, TCG and ICG -- is exactly a household name.
David Turetsky, who until recently headed the Justice Department's review of telecommunications mergers, said SBC and AT&T are likely working on a strategy to sidestep the competition problem.

"I think the companies will no doubt propose some sort of fix, or claim efficiencies, and the issues will turn on the adequacy of that," he said. "I don't think they'll contend they were unlikely to compete."
Experts said SBC could create a wholesale company that would sell services to all local telephone retailers and use a separate company to purchase the elements of local service.
At the same time, it could argue that the merger helps it muscle up for emerging heavyweight worldwide competition in the telecommunications industry.

But some critics dismiss that argument, suggesting every telephone company will be building alliances. Said one, who asked not to be identified: "It's a difficult and deceptive line of reasoning to say that American consumers in states like California ought to suffer the loss of competition and the lower productivity that comes from paying higher prices so that these companies can invest abroad."
